lessons.title: London, Euronext, and Frankfurt: Europe's Fragmented Exchange Landscape

children.text: In February 2026, AstraZeneca, one of the most valuable companies in Britain, began trading directly on the New York Stock Exchange. It kept its London listing, but the message was clear. Around the same time, the fintech company Wise shifted its primary listing from London to the US, and equipment rental giant Ashtead announced plans to do the same. Meanwhile, Paris-headquartered Euronext was busy buying exchanges, completing its takeover of the Athens Stock Exchange and renaming it Euronext Athens in April 2026. India has one securities regulator, one currency and two exchanges that share most of the same companies. Europe has dozens of exchanges, several currencies, national regulators and a pan-European trading platform that out-trades them all. This lesson untangles it.

body.text: Europe is not one stock market. It is a patchwork of national markets stitched together by a few large exchange groups and pan-European trading platforms. To read Europe, know the groups, the currencies and where trading really happens.

children.text: The Exchange Groups That Run Europe

Decades of mergers have folded most of Europe's national exchanges into a handful of groups. Each group owns several markets, and each market keeps its own flagship index and local identity. When someone says "Europe's stock market", they usually mean these five groups.

cells: Paris, Amsterdam, Milan, Brussels, Dublin, Lisbon, Oslo, Athens
Frankfurt (Xetra), plus Eurex derivatives and Clearstream settlement
Zurich, plus Madrid and other Spanish markets through BME
Stockholm, Copenhagen, Helsinki, Iceland and the Baltics

body.text: LSEG is far more than a stock exchange. It also owns FTSE Russell, the index provider you met in Chapter 1, and a huge financial data business. Deutsche Börse owns Eurex, one of the world's biggest derivatives exchanges, and Clearstream, which holds trillions of euros of securities. For these groups, running share trading is only one part of the business.

children.text: Why Europe Is So Fragmented

markDefs.definition: Markets in Financial Instruments Directive. The EU rulebook for trading venues and investment firms. It opened share trading to competition, so the same stock can trade on many venues, not just its home exchange.
Multilateral trading facility. A trading venue, other than a traditional exchange, that brings together buyers and sellers of securities under EU or UK rules. Cboe Europe runs some of the largest.

children.text: Three layers of fragmentation make Europe harder to read than India or the US. First, regulation: the EU has a coordinating authority, ESMA, but each country has its own regulator, such as AMF in France and BaFin in Germany, and the UK has gone its own way with the FCA since Brexit. Second, money: shares trade in euros, pounds, Swiss francs, Swedish, Danish and Norwegian kronor. Third, trading venues: under
MiFID
rules, a stock listed in Paris can also trade on competing platforms called
MTFs
. The result is striking: the largest share trading venue in Europe is not a national stock exchange at all, but Cboe Europe, a US-owned pan-European platform.

body.title: India vs Europe: how many moving parts?

columns.label: India
points: Two main exchanges, NSE and BSE, sharing most large companies
Two depositories, NSDL and CDSL, under one set of rules
One settlement cycle, T+1, with optional T+0 for top stocks

columns.label: Europe
points: ESMA plus national regulators in each country, and the FCA in the UK
Euro, pound, Swiss franc and three Nordic kronor
Five major exchange groups plus pan-European MTFs
Several settlement systems, including Euroclear and Clearstream
T+2 settlement today, moving to T+1 on 11 October 2027

body.title: Europe's busiest venue
body.question: Measured by share of European equity trading in Q1 2026, which venue was the largest?
body.explanation: Cboe Europe averaged 25.5% of European equity trading in Q1 2026, its highest level since 2011. Because MiFID lets European stocks trade on competing venues, a pan-European platform can handle more trading than any single national exchange, even though companies list on their home exchanges. Home exchanges still matter most for opening and closing auctions and for listings.

children.text: London: The Champion Losing Its Crown

For most of modern history, London was Europe's undisputed financial capital. Brexit, low valuations and a shortage of fast-growing technology companies have chipped away at that. Paris briefly overtook London as Europe's largest equity market in late 2022, before London won the title back in 2024 amid political turmoil in France. The bigger worry for London is companies leaving. Firms that want higher valuations and access to the deepest pool of investors increasingly choose New York, either for their main listing or alongside London.

body.text: London's problem is a lesson for India too. Companies list where they believe investors will value them most. NSE and BSE currently benefit from high domestic valuations and strong SIP inflows. If those conditions change, Indian companies with global businesses could also look abroad, especially now that rules allow direct listing of Indian companies on international exchanges at GIFT City.

children.text: Costs and Quirks: Taxes, Pence and Settlement

markDefs.definition: The pence price of a London-listed share, often shown as GBX. 100 pence make one pound, so a share quoted at 2,450 costs £24.50.

children.text: Two practical quirks catch newcomers. First, some European countries tax share purchases. Indian investors know Securities Transaction Tax, but the UK and France charge more on the buy side. Second, London quotes most share prices in
pence
, not pounds. A Shell share shown at 2,700 is £27, not £2,700. Read a London quote carelessly and every calculation is off by a factor of 100.

body.caption: Share transaction taxes: Europe vs India

cells: Purchases of shares in French companies worth over €1 billion
Securities Transaction Tax on delivery trades
Both the purchase and the sale

body.caption: Convert pence to pounds first, then apply UK stamp duty

body.title: Stamp duty on a London purchase
body.prompt: You buy 400 shares of a UK company quoted at 2,450 pence. How much UK stamp duty do you pay, in £?
body.explanation: Trade value = 2,450 × 400 ÷ 100 = £9,800. Stamp duty = £9,800 × 0.5% = £49. If you forgot the pence conversion, you would calculate a trade of £980,000 and stamp duty of £4,900. By comparison, Indian STT on a delivery purchase of the same value is 0.1%, but India also charges 0.1% when you sell, while UK stamp duty applies only on the purchase.

body.text: Europe still settles share trades on T+2, a cycle India left behind in 2023. The EU, the UK and Switzerland have agreed to move to T+1 together on 11 October 2027, so that a trade in London, Paris or Zurich settles on the same timetable.

children.text: When Europe Trades in Indian Time

body.caption: Main European trading hours in IST

body.title: The overlap window
body.textWithBlank: In summer, European markets open at 12:30 pm IST and NSE's regular session ends at 3:30 pm IST, so the two overlap for ___ hours.
body.explanation: From 12:30 pm to 3:30 pm is 3 hours. In winter, when Europe opens at 1:30 pm IST, the overlap shrinks to 2 hours. This overlap is why Europe's open often shifts the Nifty's afternoon direction, especially for metals, autos and IT stocks with European exposure.

children.text: India's Links to European Markets

markDefs.definition: Rupee-denominated bonds issued by Indian entities to overseas investors. The investor, not the Indian issuer, takes the currency risk.
Global Depositary Receipt. Like an ADR, but listed outside the US, often in London or Luxembourg, representing shares of a foreign company.

children.text: London has long been India's main gateway into European capital markets. It became the world's leading centre for
masala bonds

, starting with HDFC's issue in 2016 as the first by an Indian private company. NTPC listed a green masala bond there the same year, and Kerala's infrastructure fund KIIFB listed its debut masala bond on the London Stock Exchange in 2019. Several Indian companies have also listed
GDRs

in London. Beyond listings, European demand matters directly to Indian companies such as Infosys, which earns a large share of its revenue from Europe, and Tata Motors' passenger vehicle arm, which owns UK-based Jaguar Land Rover.

body.title: "Europe's markets are dying"
body.scenario: At a family dinner, a cousin who works in a Bengaluru tech company says: "European stock markets are finished. Everyone is leaving London for New York. There's no point even following Europe."
body.prompt: Give a balanced reply. Where is your cousin right, where are they wrong, and why should an Indian investor still watch European markets?
body.modelAnswer:
Where the cousin is right:
1. London has lost major companies and listings, including Arm choosing Nasdaq, CRH and Flutter moving their primary listings to NYSE, Wise shifting to the US and AstraZeneca adding a direct NYSE listing.
2. US markets offer deeper investor pools and often higher valuations, especially for technology companies.

Where the cousin is wrong:
1. London is not all of Europe. Euronext alone hosts over 1,800 issuers worth about €7 trillion, and Frankfurt, Zurich and the Nordic exchanges remain large.
2. Europe is home to globally dominant companies such as ASML, which makes the machines that every advanced chipmaker needs, plus Nestlé, Roche, LVMH, SAP and Novo Nordisk.
3. Many companies that add a US listing keep their European listing too.

Why an Indian investor should still watch Europe:
1. Europe opens at 12:30 pm IST in summer and often shifts the Nifty's afternoon mood.
2. Indian IT companies earn a large share of revenue from European clients, and JLR's fortunes affect Tata Motors' passenger vehicle business.
3. European central bank decisions and the euro affect global money flows, including FPI flows into India.

body.title: Read a European stock quote correctly
steps: Identify the home exchange and exchange group, for example ASML on Euronext Amsterdam.
Note the trading currency: euro, pound, Swiss franc or a Nordic krona.
If it is a London quote, check whether the price is in pence and divide by 100 to get pounds.
Check whether a purchase tax applies, such as 0.5% UK stamp duty or 0.4% French FTT.
Convert local trading hours to IST, remembering European clocks change on 25 October 2026.

points: Europe is a patchwork of national markets run by a few groups: Euronext, LSEG, Deutsche Börse, SIX and Nasdaq Nordic.
Euronext is the largest, with over 1,800 issuers worth about €7 trillion across 8 countries as of June 2026, including Athens since its 2025 takeover.

Fragmentation comes from national regulators, multiple currencies and MiFID rules that let stocks trade on competing venues. Cboe Europe handled 25.5% of European equity trading in Q1 2026, more than any national exchange.
London is losing listings to New York, with Arm, CRH, Flutter, Wise, AstraZeneca and Ashtead all choosing or adding US listings.
Watch the quirks: London prices are usually in pence, the UK charges 0.5% stamp duty on purchases and France charges 0.4% FTT on large French companies.
Europe still settles on T+2 and moves to T+1 on 11 October 2027. India has been on T+1 since January 2023.
European markets open at 12:30 pm IST in summer and 1:30 pm IST in winter, overlapping with NSE's afternoon session.
